scenes.visual: amino acid splits into carbon (burn/rebuild) and nitrogen (collect, transport, excrete)
scenes.narration: When you catabolize an amino acid, you face two separate problems. The carbon skeleton is valuable fuel that can be burned in the TCA cycle or rebuilt into glucose and fatty acids, but the amino nitrogen is a liability. Free ammonia is toxic, so the cell splits the molecule. Nitrogen is collected onto glutamate, shuttled safely through the blood as alanine and glutamine, funneled to the liver, run through the urea cycle, and excreted in urine. Carbon can be burned or rebuilt. Nitrogen must be collected, transported safely, and excreted. Keeping these two fates separate is the organizing logic of the entire chapter.

scenes.visual: many amino acids -> glutamate hub (transamination) -> free NH3 (deamination)
scenes.narration: Stripping nitrogen from most amino acids takes two moves. Step 1 is transamination. An aminotransferase hands the amino group from many different amino acids onto alpha-ketoglutarate, collecting all that nitrogen onto a single carrier, glutamate. This step is reversible and funnels diverse inputs into one channel. Step 2 is oxidative deamination. Glutamate dehydrogenase releases the nitrogen from glutamate as free ammonia, regenerating alpha-ketoglutarate to do it all again. The reaction can run both ways, but in the liver the urea cycle keeps drawing the ammonia off, so the nitrogen flows toward disposal. Many amino acids in, two moves, and free ammonia out, to be packaged as glutamine or fed to the urea cycle.

scenes.visual: muscle-blood-liver loop: alanine out, glucose back
scenes.narration: Working muscle has a clever way to ship its nitrogen home. As muscle breaks down amino acids, it transaminates the nitrogen onto pyruvate to make alanine. Alanine is non-toxic, so it travels safely through the blood to the liver. There the liver strips the nitrogen back off, feeding it into the urea cycle, and converts the leftover pyruvate into glucose. That glucose returns to the muscle as fuel. So alanine is the nitrogen shuttle, and glucose is the energy shuttle. Running in opposite directions. The muscle offloads its waste nitrogen and gets fuel back in the same elegant round trip.

scenes.visual: glutamine carries two N from tissues to liver, kidney, gut/immune
scenes.narration: Glutamine is the workhorse of nitrogen transport and the most abundant free amino acid in your blood. Tissues everywhere add ammonia onto glutamate's side chain to make glutamine, which carries two nitrogens safely and without toxicity. The bloodstream then delivers it where it is needed. The liver for urea synthesis, the kidney for acid-base balance, and rapidly dividing cells like those in the gut and immune system that use glutamine as fuel and as a building block. Ammonia is toxic, so the body keeps it low in the general blood. Much nitrogen travels as glutamine, the safe, abundant, two-nitrogen courier.

scenes.visual: urea cycle + TCA cycle as two linked wheels
scenes.narration: Here is an analogy that makes the liver's chemistry click. Picture a bicycle with two wheels that share a chain. One wheel is the urea cycle, the other is the TCA cycle, and they are physically linked through shared intermediates like fumarate and aspartate. When you pedal, both wheels turn together. Urea comes out one side as the nitrogen waste product, and glucose-building carbon comes out the other. The liver runs both wheels at once. Dispose of nitrogen as urea while reclaiming carbon for energy and glucose. Nitrogen out one side, glucose out the other, one connected machine doing two jobs.
